findings.current: I used to win his daughter.
findings.issue: Across the line break ("what mighty magic / ... / I used to win") the modern reader will parse "used to" as habitual past ("I used to win her"), which garbles the key clause "what charms ... I used to win his daughter".
findings.proposed: I used in winning his daughter.

findings.original: She never yet was foolish that was fair,
findings.current: No pretty woman was ever so foolish she couldn't get by,
findings.issue: Iago's paradox is that no beautiful woman is ever foolish, because her folly (wantonness) gets her an heir; "couldn't get by" replaces the claim and blunts the paradox Desdemona then names.
findings.proposed: No pretty woman was ever really foolish,

findings.original: (For I fear Cassio with my night-cap too)
findings.current: (because I suspect Cassio with my wife too, in my nightcap),
findings.issue: "in my nightcap" dangles and can read as Iago wearing it; the image is Cassio having worn Iago's nightcap, i.e. been in his bed.
findings.proposed: (because I suspect Cassio has worn my nightcap too — been in my bed),

findings.original: To change the cod's head for the salmon's tail;
findings.current: as to swap a cod's head for a salmon's tail — trade solid worth for a cheap thrill;
findings.issue: The added gloss commits to one contested reading and drops the bawdy undertone (cod = penis, tail = pudendum) that fits Iago's run of sexual jokes.
findings.proposed: as to swap a cod's head for a salmon's tail — trade a good thing for a worse, or one sex organ for another;

findings.original: Therefore my hopes, not surfeited to death,
findings.current: so my hopes, not yet sickened to death by too much fear,
findings.issue: "surfeited" means overfed or glutted (hopes not so excessive as to sicken); "by too much fear" adds a cause the line does not state.
findings.proposed: so my hopes, not so overfed that they sicken and die,

findings.original: With such loud reason to the Cyprus wars,
findings.current: with such loud agreement, on the Cyprus wars,
findings.issue: "loud reason" is a pressing, obvious cause or public necessity rather than "agreement"; the gloss is arguable but shifts the sense.
findings.proposed: for such loud and pressing reasons, to the Cyprus wars,

findings.original: What a full fortune does the thick-lips owe,
findings.current: What a stroke of luck the thick-lips has coming to him
findings.issue: "owe" means own or possess, so the luck is already his; "has coming to him" suggests something future or deserved.
findings.proposed: What a stroke of luck the thick-lips has in his hands

findings.original: Blest fig's end! the wine she drinks is made of grapes: if she had been blessed, she would never have loved the Moor. Blessed pudding! Didst thou not see her paddle with the palm of his hand? Didst not mark that?
findings.current: Blessed, my backside! The wine she drinks is made of grapes like anyone else's. If she were so blessed, she would never have loved the Moor. Blessed pudding! Didn't you see her fondle the palm of his hand? Didn't you notice that?
findings.issue: "fig's end" (the obscene fig gesture) is swapped for "my backside"; that works as a dismissal, but the fig image is lost, and Iago has already used "a fig" in 3.82.
findings.proposed: Blessed, my fig's end — the fig I give that! The wine she drinks is made of grapes like anyone else's. If she were so blessed, she would never have loved the Moor. Blessed pudding! Didn't you see her fondle the palm of his hand? Didn't you notice that?

findings.original: Marry, before your ladyship, I grant,
findings.current: Oh, in front of your ladyship, I admit,
findings.issue: The guide sets "marry" to "why," or "indeed"; "Oh" is off-convention.
findings.proposed: Why, in front of your ladyship, I admit,
